paper_title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/.

sections.content: BiDex-100: Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks Yong Wang1,, Kecheng Zheng2, Xing Zhu2, Chao Xu1, Yujun Shen2, and Shengze Cai1, 1Zhejiang University 2Ant Group https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/ Fig. 1: Overview of BiDex-100. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/. Keywords Vision-Language-Action Models, Imitation Learning, Simulation Benchmark, Bimanual Robotics, Dexterous Manipulation I. INTRODUCTION Bimanual dexterous manipulation, the coordinated control of two multi-fingered hands acting on shared workspace, is widely regarded as prerequisite for general-purpose household and industrial robots. The past two years have brought this capability within reach: VLA models [1], [2], [3], [4], [5] now absorb large-scale demonstrations and generalize across scenes, objects, and instructions. What has not kept pace is our ability to measure where such policies actually fail. As training corpora grow, average success on narrow pickand-place suites saturates, and the discriminating power of benchmark shifts away from task coverage toward capability edges: remembering scene state, sustaining long horizons, obeying instructions that change mid-episode, learning from few demonstrations, and degrading gracefully under visual and geometric shift. 58-DoF bimanual dexterous system amplifies every one of these edges relative to the 7-DoF gripper platforms that dominate current evaluation. Its action space is high-dimensional and redundant, its success hinges on contact-rich finger coordination, and its failure modes are invisible to binary success rate. Existing manipulation benchmarks leave this gap open in three distinct ways. First, the widely used suites, among them Meta-World [6], RLBench [7], LIBERO [8], CALVIN [9], RoboCasa [10], and ManiSkill [11], are built around single arms terminated by parallel-jaw grippers, so the entire dexterity dimension is abstracted away. Second, dexteroushand benchmarks such as Bi-DexHands [12] and DexMV [13] target reinforcement learning from scratch on small task sets, without language grounding, large-scale demonstrations, or automated compositional scoring. Third, even recent largescale efforts, such as RoboTwin [14], [15] and RoboDojo [16], evaluate bimanual gripper platforms and report largely binary success, while the community has converged on the need for capability-targeted diagnosis of memory, long-horizon competence, and instruction fidelity that binary scores cannot provide. In short, the field lacks benchmark that simultaneously offers bimanual dexterous hands, capabilityorganized task suite with progress-based predicate scoring, matched In-Domain and Out-of-Domain evaluation, and large teleoperated demonstration dataset released alongside the benchmark. To address this gap, we introduce BiDex-100, MuJoCo benchmark of 106 bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks spanning five capability axes. BiDex-100 is built on simple premise: as average task success improves, evaluation should reveal not only whether policy succeeds, but also what it can do reliably and where it fails. Our contributions are: 1) capability-based benchmark for bimanual dexterity. The 106 tasks measure Generalization, Instruction-Following, Limited Demonstrations, Long Horizon, and Memory. These axes expose distinct limitations of VLA policies. Results therefore form capability profile rather than single aggregate score. 2) Matched In-Domain (ID) and Out-of-Domain (OOD) evaluation. Each task has reproducible OOD counterpart with controlled changes to appearance, scene layout, distractors, object scale, and left-right configuration. This design makes in-domain performance and robustness directly comparable. 3) large-scale dataset and reference study. We provide 8,080 success-validated teleoperation episodes, covering 6.25M frames of data across the 106 released tasks. We also evaluate 7 recent VLA models under unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. II. RELATED WORK a) Manipulation benchmarks.: The fields standard suites measure gripper-based manipulation. Meta-World [6] and RLBench [7] offer 50100 tasks for meta-RL and fewshot learning. LIBERO [8] studies lifelong transfer across 130 tasks. CALVIN [9] targets language-conditioned longhorizon chains. RoboCasa [10] and BEHAVIOR-1K [17] scale scene and activity diversity. ManiSkill2 [11] and VLABench [18] emphasize generalizable skills and language grounding. SimplerEnv [19] aligns simulation with realworld policy rankings. All of these terminate the arm in parallel-jaw gripper and score success binarily. RoboTwin [14] and RoboTwin 2.0 [15] move to bimanual grippers with generative digital twins and strong domain randomization, and RoboDojo [16] organizes 60 gripper tasks along capability dimensions with unified sim-and-real protocol, but neither exercises multi-fingered dexterity, and their scoring remains predominantly binary. DexJoCo [20] is bimanual dexterous benchmark with teleoperated demonstrations and matched ID/OOD variants, but only 11 tasks, binary scoring. BiDex100 extends the design to 106 capability-organized tasks with progress-based predicate scoring. BiDex-100 occupies the vacant corner of this design space (Table I): bimanual 22DoF dexterous hands, five capability axes, progress-based predicate scoring, and matched ID/OOD evaluation. b) Dexterous manipulation and teleoperation.: Dexterous-hand benchmarks historically trade breadth for fidelity: early Shadow-Hand suites [21] cover handful of canonical tasks; Bi-DexHands [12] provides RL environments for two Shadow hands without demonstrations or language; DexMV [13] retargets human videos but offers no standardized compositional scoring. Demonstrations for such systems depend on teleoperation: DexPilot [22] and AnyTeleop [23] retarget visual hand tracking, TeleMoMa [24] composes input modalities, Open-TeleVision [25] streams immersive headmounted video, and FACTR [26] adds low-cost force-aware exoskeleton. BiDex-100 adopts the last two modalities and unifies them through single optimization-based retargeting stack (Section IV-A). c) Vision-language-action models.: VLAs fine-tune webscale vision-language backbones into action policies [1], [2], [27], with recent designs adding flow-matching or diffusion action experts for high-frequency dexterous control [3], [4], [5]. Their published evaluations concentrate on gripper embodiments, and cross-model comparisons are complicated by per-paper protocols, action spaces, and data mixtures. TABLE I: Benchmark comparison. III. THE BIDEX-100 BENCHMARK A. Design Principles Three principles guide BiDex-100. (1) Dexterity is the object of study. Tasks require dexterous hands for skills beyond conventional grippers, such as hammering nails and watering. (2) Diagnose capabilities, not tasks. Tasks are organized by the capability they stress, namely visual and geometric generalization, instruction fidelity, data efficiency, horizon depth, and latent-state memory, rather than by scene or object type. leaderboard position therefore decomposes into an interpretable capability profile. (3) Scores must be reproducible and comparable. Machine-checkable predicate conjunctions, deterministic seeded evaluation, progress-based subtask credit, and matched ID/OOD variants replace human raters and per-paper protocols. B. Embodiments and Interfaces BiDex-100 supports two robot embodiments with the same dexterous hand design  (Fig. 1)  . The dual Franka platform consists of two 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arms [28] mounted on shared base, each equipped with 22-DoF Dexterous hand [29]. It has 58-DoF action space and executes 96 of the 106 task specifications. The remaining 10 Generalization tasks execute on the Astribot S1 humanoid [30], which shares the same hands on two 7-DoF arms. Every task is evaluated on its designated embodiment under the unified protocol; consequently, the Generalization column in Tables IIIIV aggregates 30 dual-Franka and 10 Astribot tasks. Observations include synchronized RGB-D images from head, left-wrist, and right-wrist cameras at 480 360 resolution and 25 Hz, together with proprioceptive states. The latter include arm and hand joint positions and velocities, as well as absolute end-effector poses. Actions are 58-dimensional joint targets, Fig. 2: Action Space Visualization. (a) Top-view log-density of end-effector positions across all 8,080 demonstrations; the two hands partition but substantially overlap the shared workspace, forcing bimanual coordination. (b) Per-joint usage of the bimanual 44 hand DoF, shown as median and 595% band; all five fingers engage, and thumb CMC and finger MCP joints carry the largest excursions. tgt tgt , qhand ut = [qarm ], executed by position-controlled actuators. End-effector control is also available and is converted to joint targets through inverse kinematics. Simulation runs in MuJoCo [31] at 500 Hz, with control at 25 Hz. The dexterous hands are central to BiDex-100. Fig. 3 visualizes the Memory task pour ice into cups by overlaying solid hand and object snapshots with time-gradient fingertip trajectories and markers that terminate at the pour instant. The right hand lifts and tilts the source cup above the recipient to transfer the ice ball while both hands coordinate within centimeters and reconfigure among open-palm transport, precision pinch, and power grasp. Fig. 2(a) shows that the end effectors partition but substantially overlap shared workspace, and Fig. 2(b) shows substantial motion across every finger. Fig. 4 reveals that the bimanual posture follows low-dimensional manifold: eight principal components capture 80% of postural variance, indicating compact set of reusable grasp synergies. C. Baselines and Training Protocol We benchmark seven recent VLA models spanning the major action-expert designs (Table II): π0.5 [4], GR00TN1.7 [5], InternVLA-A1.5 [36], Galaxea G0.5 [37], OpenDMDM05 [38], LingBot-VLA-v2 [39], and Xiaomi XR1 [40]. Their official checkpoints are co-trained by jointly sampling one mixture of demonstrations from all 106 tasks and five axes, using the same 58-DoF joint-space interface. Optimizer, schedule, freezing strategy, and training steps follow each models official configuration. When an action head mismatches the interface, its projection layers are resized and re-initialized by the models standard procedure. VI. CONCLUSION We presented BiDex-100, simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation with 106 declaratively specified tasks across five capability axes, two 22-DoF embodiments, progress-based predicate scoring, matched ID/OOD evaluation, and 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations. The five-axis design emphasizes capability edges as average-case skill improves, with progress-based scoring revealing differences hidden by binary success. Evaluating seven contemporary VLA models under one protocol establishes reference baselines and diagnostic capability profiles, robustness gaps, and low-data regimes. The rigidbody tabletop setting leaves sim-to-real transfer and richer physical phenomena to future work. We release all code, tasks, data, and evaluation tooling.

Each spawn region defines center, an xy-extent, and yaw range; at reset, every assigned object is placed at pose sampled uniformly from its region, so initial conditions differ across episodes even within one seed family. surface-contact flag places objects resting on the support surface rather than dropping them. b) Subtask latching and scoring.: At each control step all predicates are evaluated, and subtask latches the first time all of its predicates hold simultaneously. Let ℓk(T ) denote this latched state, mk indicate that the subtask has must-hold predicate, hk(T ) denote its terminal truth, and vk(T ) indicate latched violation. Its effective completion is ek(T ) = ℓk(T )(1 mk + mkhk(T ))(1 vk(T )). Strict success is (cid:81) wkek(T ), where wk 0 and (cid:80) wk = 100. Zero-weight safety or terminal constraints still participate in strict success. For ordered tasks, the evaluator permits subtask to latch only after the required earlier subtasks or groups have latched, enforcing the intended staging. ek(T ) and the progress score is (cid:80) c) Language schedules.: Instruction-Following switch tasks declare an ordered schedule of instruction segments. Each nonfinal segment specifies an until_step control-step boundary, while the last segment supplies the instruction for the remainder of the episode. The policy observation receives the active segment text. Scoring continues to use the tasks declared predicate set, with ordered subtasks enforcing the intended sequence. d) Episode horizon.: task-level max_steps value takes precedence when present. Otherwise, the evaluation horizon is 1.2 the 90th-percentile demonstration length in control steps, with 30 fallback when no demonstration lengths are available. OUT-OF-DOMAIN TRANSFORMATION RULES Each in-domain task is paired with single out-of-domain (OOD) variant that perturbs the scene but keeps the goal unchanged, so the OOD score isolates robustness rather than task mastery. Transformations are deterministic and reproducible across runs and machines through stable, component-scoped keys. Six transformation families are used: 1) Scene randomization (all tasks): floor, wall, and tabletop textures resampled from held-out pool; light position and diffuse intensity jittered; shadow casting toggled. 2) Camera variation (all tasks): head and wrist camera extrinsics selected from validated finite pose bank for each evaluation key. 3) Layout variation (all tasks): task-specific placement and geometry changes are recorded in the committed OOD YAML. 4) Distractor injection (45 compatible tasks): three to nine objects are placed in collision-safe tabletop regions; grasping distractor terminates the episode at its current score, so OOD scores penalize both distraction and mis-grasping. 5) Object rescaling (ten articulated Limited-Demonstrations tasks): each OOD YAML selects smaller or larger regime anchored by factor in {0.85, 0.9, 1.1, 1.15}. deterministic episode factor is sampled within 0.18 of the anchor and clipped to [0.65, 0.96] for smaller regimes or [1.04, 1.35] for larger regimes. 6) Left-right mirroring (nine tasks): task geometry is mirrored about the workspace midline to exchange arm-side demands. At evaluation time the OOD variant is loaded in place of the base task. The committed YAML fixes the layout and applicable transformations, while appearance, camera, articulated scale, and distractor placement are derived reproducibly from the task, seed, and episode. The goal, episode count, horizon, and scoring rules are shared across domains. In-domain evaluation samples recorded working robot pose and restores only the robot joints, while retaining fresh base-YAML object placement. OOD evaluation uses the default robot reset pose with the committed OOD placement. Each domain is deterministic and identical across models. X. Object placements are sampled from the applicable task regions with seed that is deterministic function of the task, seed index, and episode index. The ID protocol additionally restores deterministically selected working robot pose, while OOD uses the default robot reset pose. This procedure makes every rollout reproducible within its domain. Episodes terminate on full success, on timeout (explicit task max_steps, otherwise 1.2 the P90 demonstration length), or, in OOD scenes with distractors, on grasping distractor object. The vectorized harness co-locates policy inference and simulation with single shared renderer per worker. b) Metrics.: Per episode we record strict success, the progress score (as defined in the main paper), the per-subtask latch times, and the time-to-first-failure. DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS The five-axis organization reflects deliberate benchmark design. As VLA training data grows, average-case skill becomes less discriminative, while memory, horizon, instruction fidelity, data efficiency, and robustness remain capability edges. Progress-based predicate scoring makes the heterogeneous tasks commensurable, exposes partial progress when strict success is not reached, and keeps evaluation fully automated. The resulting per-axis vectors show whether short-horizon competence extends to memory and long-horizon tasks. ID/OOD gaps measure aggregate robustness under the combined scripted shifts, and Limited-Demonstrations isolates acquisition from 30 examples. BiDex-100 is rigid-body benchmark. MuJoCo does not model fluids, deformable objects, or rich frictional contact at the fidelity of hardware, and sim-to-real transfer of policies trained on the released demonstrations remains to be validated on the physical platforms. The object library, while diverse, is centered on tabletop food and kitchen scenes. The OOD shifts are scripted and finite; learned or adversarially generated shift distributions are natural extension. Within this scope, evaluating seven contemporary VLA models under one protocol establishes reference baselines and diagnostic framework of capability profiles, ID/OOD robustness gaps, and low-data regimes. We release the code, tasks, data, and evaluation tooling to support reproducible community use.
